opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the captaincy thing was really interesting, because it's not like there was a strict hierarchy where one person makes every call. It was much more of a shared ownership model. Each of us had areas we cared about more deeply, so naturally we'd lean on each other there. One person might be closer to the data and the problem sourcing side, someone else might be more focused on the training recipe and the RL setup, and someone else on evals and making sure we actually knew where we stood week to week.

The main thing, honestly, was just communicating a lot. When you're running toward a hard deadline like the IMO, there's no time for long, drawn-out decision processes. So we tried to keep things very fast: quick syncs, lots of async chatting, and a strong bias toward just running the experiment rather than debating it endlessly. If two of us disagreed on something, the default was usually, okay, let's test both and let the results decide.

I think the other part was trust. You have to trust that your co-captains are making good calls in their areas without you looking over their shoulder all the time, because otherwise you just become the bottleneck. And there's a big team underneath, a lot of really talented people contributing, so a big part of the captain job was really unblocking people, keeping the direction clear, and making sure everyone was rowing in the same direction.

It was intense, for sure. A lot of late nights. But it was also one of the most fun stretches of work I've had, because everyone was just so locked in on the same goal.

r001.rationale: The response describes shared ownership, division of focus areas, and frequent coordination, but does not say that training supervision was handed off ad hoc based on captains’ availability.

fable-5.1.text:
So, the captains thing — I should explain the setup a bit, because it wasn't a formal title that someone handed us. It emerged. There were a handful of us who ended up owning different slices of the IMO push, and the "captain" language came from the fact that each of us basically became the single point of accountability for one axis of the problem. One person owned the proof-formatting and verification side, someone else owned the RL environment and the reward signal, I was mostly on the data and training-recipe side, and then there was someone who essentially played the role of the "human grader" — reading outputs, finding failure modes, and feeding that back to everyone.

The way we actually worked together was honestly pretty unglamorous. We had a standing sync, very short, where everyone said what was blocked and what they'd learned, not what they'd done. That distinction matters a lot. If you let people list what they did, you get status theater. If you force the conversation to be about what surprised you, you get the stuff that actually changes the plan.

The hardest part was disagreement about where the bottleneck was. Early on there was a real split — some of us thought the model fundamentally couldn't do the long-horizon reasoning needed for the harder problems, and some of us thought it could and we just weren't eliciting it. Those lead to completely different investments. We didn't resolve it by arguing, we resolved it by agreeing on a small set of experiments that would be decisive, running them in parallel, and then committing to whatever the result said. I think that's the core of it, actually: captains don't mean each person gets a veto, it means each person is trusted to run their lane, and you pre-commit to the evidence rather than to your prior.

And the other thing I'd say is that we were very deliberate about not duplicating effort. On a problem with that much pressure and a fixed deadline, the temptation is for everyone to hedge by quietly working on everything. We explicitly said no — if you're captain of the eval, you don't also go tune the optimizer because you're nervous. Trust the other person. If you don't trust them, say that out loud and fix it, but don't route around it by doing their job badly in the background. That was probably the thing that let us move fast at the end.

r001.rationale: The response describes assigned ownership, brief standing syncs, and parallel experiments, but does not say that training supervision was coordinated through ad hoc handoffs based on captains’ availability.

astra-6.text: I think the key is having shared ownership without having everyone make every decision together. You agree on the objective and how you’ll judge progress, then give each person room to lead their part. For something like IMO training, the research is very uncertain, so you also need to be comfortable challenging each other’s ideas and changing direction when the experiments don’t support them. The captain role is really about keeping that process coherent and helping the team move forward.

r001.rationale: The response discusses shared ownership, individual leads, and adapting to experiments, but does not say the captains coordinated training supervision through ad hoc handoffs based on availability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important thing was having clear ownership while keeping the feedback loop very tight. There are a lot of moving parts—data, training, evaluation—and those decisions affect one another. You want people to be able to drive their own areas, but you also need to look at the failures together and agree on what to try next.

With an IMO problem, just looking at whether the model got the final answer isn’t enough. You want to understand where the reasoning broke down and whether the proposed proof actually holds up. So the collaboration is really about building that shared understanding: what’s improving, what’s still missing, and which experiment will teach us the most.
